- **Authors / year:** Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan, Ameet Deshpande — 2023 (arXiv v1) / KDD 2024 (v3, 28 Jun 2024)

text:
- **Authors / year:** Andrea Volpini, Elie Raad, Beatrice Gamba, David Riccitelli (WordLift) — 2026 (arXiv:2603.10700v1, 11 Mar 2026)
- **File:** `VolpiniEtAl-2026-StructuredLinkedData-RAG.pdf` · 33 pages · 908,930 bytes

- **Contents:** Controlled 3×2 experiment (2,443 evals, 4 domains; Vertex AI Vector Search + Google ADK): Schema.org JSON-LD alone gives only a modest gain (Δ +0.17, p_adj = 0.024), while enhanced entity pages (linked data + llms.txt-style agent instructions + breadcrumbs) give +29.6% accuracy in standard RAG and +29.8% in agentic RAG (p < 10⁻²¹, d ≈ 0.60).
- **TRANSFER:** The most decision-useful schema result on the shelf: for GSE, plain JSON-LD is a minor lever — the measured win is full entity pages with typed relationships (players, teams, games, picks as linked entities) that an agent can traverse, which maps straight onto GSE's projections/rankings surface and its research-arm knowledge graph.

section: A3-1 — Target 1: Fogg Behavior Model
title: A3-1 — Target 1: Fogg Behavior Model
text:
**"A Behavior Model for Persuasive Design" — B.J. Fogg (2009)**
Persuasive '09 conference paper, ACM. 7 pp, 535,187 bytes.
**File:** `Fogg-2009-BehaviorModelPersuasiveDesign.pdf`
**Source:** https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1145%252F100216.100217.zip/10.1145%252F1541948.1541999.pdf (Archive.org scholarly-sources corpus copy of the ACM paper, DOI 10.1145/1541948.1541999; the current behaviormodel.org homepage no longer links the PDF — see Gaps note).
**Contents:** Behavior = Motivation × Ability × Trigger, all three converging at the same moment; motivator pairs (pleasure/pain, hope/fear, social acceptance/rejection), six simplicity factors under Ability, and trigger types — the design grammar for any page that asks for an action.
**TRANSFER:** Audit every GSE package page against B=MAT: motivation is highest right after a winning pick / big game (trigger timing), Ability is checkout friction (clicks, form fields, payment steps), and the Trigger must fire at that peak moment — a subscribe prompt buried on a generic page wastes the one moment all three factors align.

title: A3-2 — Target 2a: Fogg credibility research (large study)
text:
**"How Do People Evaluate a Web Site's Credibility? Results from a Large Study" — B.J. Fogg, Cathy Soohoo, David Danielson, Leslie Marable, Julianne Stanford & Ellen R. Tauber (2002)**
Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab / Consumer WebWatch report, released Oct 29, 2002. 99 pp, 736,345 bytes.
**File:** `FoggEtAl-2002-HowPeopleEvaluateWebSiteCredibility.pdf`
**Source:** https://credibility.stanford.edu/pdf/How_Do_People_Evaluate_a_Web_Site's_Credibility_v37.pdf (Stanford credibility.stanford.edu, the lab's own posting).
**Contents:** 2,684 people evaluated live websites; "design look" was the most-mentioned credibility factor (46.1% of comments), ahead of information structure and information focus — people judge credibility from surface design first, not from stated credentials.
**TRANSFER:** For a paywalled picks site asking strangers for money, visual design IS the credibility argument: layout, typography, and consistency on the package pages will be read as proof of competence before any record or methodology is — design polish is not decoration, it is the first trust test the site either passes or fails.

section: A3-3 — Target 2b: Fogg credibility research (theory)
title: A3-3 — Target 2b: Fogg credibility research (theory)
text:
**"Prominence-Interpretation Theory: Explaining How People Assess Credibility" — B.J. Fogg (2002)**
Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab working paper, v1 July 12, 2002, updated Oct 25, 2002. 5 pp, 34,648 bytes.
**File:** `Fogg-2002-ProminenceInterpretationTheory.pdf`
**Source:** http://credibility.stanford.edu/pdf/p-iTheory_Fogg_Oct02.pdf (Stanford credibility.stanford.edu, the lab's own posting).
**Contents:** Credibility impact = Prominence × Interpretation: an element only affects trust if it is (1) noticed and (2) judged favorably; prominence is driven most by user involvement, then topic, task, and experience.
**TRANSFER:** A trust element nobody notices does nothing — GSE's record, sourcing, and honesty signals must be placed where a motivated visitor actually looks on the package page (near price and subscribe button), not parked on an About page; and each noticed element must be interpretable in one glance or it scores zero.
urls: http://credibility.stanford.edu/pdf/p-iTheory_Fogg_Oct02.pdf

**"The Effect of Electronic Word-of-Mouth on Sales: A Meta-Analytic Review of Platform, Product, and Metric Factors" — Ana Babić Rosario, Francesca Sotgiu, Kristine de Valck & Tammo H.A. Bijmolt (2016)**
*Journal of Marketing Research* 53(3), 297–318, DOI 10.1509/jmr.14.0380. 23 pp (incl. repository cover), 474,105 bytes.

**Contents:** Meta-analysis of 1,532 effect sizes across 96 studies, 40 platforms, 26 product categories: eWOM is positively correlated with sales (r ≈ .091) on average, volume of word-of-mouth moves sales more than valence, and effects are stronger when receivers can judge their similarity to senders (homophily).
**TRANSFER:** On GSE's site, member-count and testimonial VOLUME beats a few glowing quotes, and testimonials convert best when the reader can see the reviewer is like them (same sport, same package tier, same bankroll level) — collect many short, identified-by-profile member results rather than three polished endorsements.

title: A3-5 — Target 4: Scarcity meta-analysis
text:
**"Scarcity Tactics in Marketing: A Meta-Analysis of Product Scarcity Effects on Consumer Purchase Intentions" — Belinda Barton, Natalina Zlatevska & Harmen Oppewal (2022)**
*Journal of Retailing* 98(4), 741–758, DOI 10.1016/j.jretai.2022.06.003. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). 18 pp, 933,214 bytes.
**File:** `BartonZlatevskaOppewal-2022-ScarcityTacticsMetaAnalysis.pdf`
**Source:** https://researchmgt.monash.edu/ws/files/423908416/392343368_oa.pdf (Monash University repository, publisher's open-access version).
**Contents:** Meta-analysis of 416 effect sizes from 131 studies: scarcity cues raise purchase intentions, but the type must match the product — demand-based scarcity works best for utilitarian products, supply-based scarcity for experiences, time-based scarcity for high-involvement products.
**TRANSFER:** GSE packages are high-involvement experiences, so the evidence-backed levers are time-based (enrollment closes before kickoff / price rises Monday) and supply-based (capped member slots) scarcity — not generic "only X left" demand claims, which this meta-analysis says are the weakest match for this product type and the easiest to read as fake.
urls: https://researchmgt.monash.edu/ws/files/423908416/392343368_oa.pdf

section: A3-6 — Target 5a: Referral rewards and receiver responses
title: A3-6 — Target 5a: Referral rewards and receiver responses
text:
**"Receiver Responses to Rewarded Referrals: The Motive Inferences Framework" (manuscript title: "All Referrals Are Not Created Equal") — Peeter W.J. Verlegh, Gangseog Ryu, Mirjam A. Tuk & Lawrence Feick (2013)**
*Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science* (author manuscript, conditionally-accepted version). 44 pp, 261,994 bytes.
**File:** `VerleghRyuTukFeick-2013-RewardedReferralsReceiverResponses.pdf`
**Source:** https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/cc65e63e-06f9-4c8a-862c-8996b832e525/content (Imperial College London Spiral repository, author manuscript).
**Contents:** Paying only the referrer backfires with receivers: they infer an ulterior motive and respond worse, especially for unsolicited and weak-tie referrals; rewarding BOTH sides, or using symbolic rewards, eliminates the negative effect.
**TRANSFER:** GSE's referral program must be two-sided by design — "give a free week, get a free week" — never a referrer-only commission a friend can discover later; a one-sided bounty makes every member's recommendation read as a sales pitch and taxes exactly the trust that makes referrals convert.

section: A3-7 — Target 5b: Referral reward structure, field experiment
title: A3-7 — Target 5b: Referral reward structure, field experiment
text:
**"Can Reward Uncertainty Encourage Social Referrals? Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment" — Andy Tao Li, Rodrigo Belo & Ting Li (2025)**
Author-posted manuscript, September 12, 2025. 87 pp, 1,472,603 bytes.
**File:** `LiBeloLi-2025-RewardUncertaintySocialReferrals.pdf`
**Source:** https://rodrigobelo.com/assets/pdf/reward-uncertainty.pdf (co-author's own site).
**Contents:** Randomized field experiment on 160,000+ users of a Chinese telecom operator: uncertain (lottery-style) rewards for the SENDER plus a certain reward for the RECIPIENT raised total referrals 20.9%; uncertainty on the recipient's side cut referrals 12.3%, via perceived unfairness on the receiving end.
**TRANSFER:** Precise split for GSE referral design: keep the new member's reward fixed and guaranteed (e.g., locked first-month discount — certainty is what makes them act), and put any gamification on the referrer's side only (chance at a free month), where uncertainty helps instead of hurting.

section: A3-8 — Target 6: Sponsorship/affiliate disclosure effects
title: A3-8 — Target 6: Sponsorship/affiliate disclosure effects
text:
**"The Paradox of (Dis)trust in Sponsorship Disclosure: The Characteristics and Effects of Sponsored Online Consumer Reviews" — Su Jung Kim, Ewa Maslowska & Ali Tamaddoni (2019)**
*Decision Support Systems* 116, 114–124, DOI 10.1016/j.dss.2018.10.014. 11 pp, 613,258 bytes.
**File:** `KimMaslowskaTamaddoni-2019-SponsorshipDisclosureParadox.pdf`
**Source:** https://spiegel.medill.northwestern.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2021/07/KimMaslowskaTamaddoni-2019-DSS.pdf (author-posted via Northwestern Medill Spiegel Center).
**Contents:** Text-mining plus a randomized experiment: disclosing sponsorship raises suspicion of ulterior motives and lowers attitudes/purchase intention for POSITIVE reviews, but does not hurt (and can help) when the review is negative or mixed — disclosure damage depends on review valence and reviewer credibility.
**TRANSFER:** For GSE affiliate and partner placements (sportsbook links, sponsor mentions), disclosure is legally required and this paper prices it: expect a conversion cost on straight promotional copy, offset by keeping disclosed content specific and mixed (real pros/cons, named limits) rather than uniformly glowing — uniform praise plus a disclosure label is the exact combination readers punish.

section: A3-9 — Target 7: Charm / just-below pricing, preregistered experiments
title: A3-9 — Target 7: Charm / just-below pricing, preregistered experiments
text:
**"How Consumers Evaluated Precise, Just-Below, and Round Prices: Evidence from Two High-Powered, Preregistered Experiments" — Yannik A. Escher, Eve Sarah Troll, Marie-Lena Henjes & David D. Loschelder (2026)**
*Frontiers in Behavioral Economics* 5:1828446, DOI 10.3389/frbhe.2026.1828446. Open access (CC BY). 10 pp, 568,545 bytes.
**File:** `EscherEtAl-2026-PreciseJustBelowRoundPrices.pdf`
**Source:** https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/behavioral-economics/articles/10.3389/frbhe.2026.1828446/pdf (journal open-access PDF).
**Contents:** Two preregistered, high-powered experiments (N=729) comparing round ($10.00), just-below ($9.99), and precise ($9.87) prices: precise prices produced the most favorable price image and the most underestimation in recall, followed by just-below, then round — a modern, replication-grade check on the classic $9-ending claim.
**TRANSFER:** GSE package pricing should be tested, not assumed: the classic charm ending is not the strongest option in this evidence — a precise price (e.g., $47 rather than $49.99 or $50) can read as more honest and more favorable for a data product, which fits a brand selling analysis rather than hype; A/B the three endings on the package page.

title: 6. Modelling the HRV Response to Training Loads in Elite Rugby Sevens Players — Sean Williams, Stephen West, Dan Howells, Simon P.T. Kemp, Andrew A. Flatt, Keith Stokes (J. Sports Science & Medicine, 2018, 17:402–408)

- **Contents:** Fits the Banister two-component impulse-response (fitness–fatigue) model to daily training loads and predicts chronic HRV (Ln rMSSD) out-of-sample; internal load (sRPE) markedly outperforms external load (high-speed distance) as the model input — 7 of 8 athletes met validity criteria with sRPE vs 1 of 8 with HSD.

section: 1. Stanford University — US 6,285,999 B1 (2001) — 12 pp
title: 1. Stanford University — US 6,285,999 B1 (2001) — 12 pp
text:
**"Method for Node Ranking in a Linked Database"** (the PageRank patent; inventor Lawrence Page; assignee: Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University). File: `Stanford-US6285999-PageRank.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Scores linked documents by iteratively propagating rank through the link graph — a document's score is a function of the scores of documents linking to it, normalized by their out-link counts — with a random-surfer damping component so rank converges on the whole database. The claims cover the scoring method itself, not any query-time interface.
- TRANSFER: The original authority-from-graph-structure algorithm. Directly reusable thinking for GSE: any internal corpus (papers, repos, accounts) can be ranked by citation/link endorsement rather than by self-description — the anti-guru filter in computable form. Also the math ancestor of the engine's network-centrality work already in the library (Barabási).

title: 2. Google Inc. — US 8,938,463 B1 (2015) — 24 pp
text:
**"Modifying Search Result Ranking Based on Implicit User Feedback and a Model of Presentation Bias."** File: `Google-US8938463-ImplicitFeedbackPresentationBias.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Builds a query-independent *prior model* of result selection from click/selection data spanning many queries, conditioned on presentation-bias features (result rank, etc.), and hands that prior to the ranking engine so implicit-feedback re-ranking is normalized — separating "users clicked it because it was good" from "users clicked it because it was shown first." This is the granted patent behind Google's long-click/short-click ranking family.
- TRANSFER: The bias-correction pattern is the transferable asset: any GSE surface that learns from clicks (site search, content ordering, pick-page engagement) inherits position bias unless the selection model is debiased exactly this way. Same math applies to grading which content "performed" — raw CTR on position 1 is not evidence of quality.

section: 3. Microsoft Corporation — US 7,664,735 B2 (2010) — 14 pp
title: 3. Microsoft Corporation — US 7,664,735 B2 (2010) — 14 pp
text:
**"Method and System for Ranking Documents of a Search Result to Improve Diversity and Information Richness"** (inventors incl. Benyu Zhang, Zheng Chen, Wei-Ying Ma). File: `Microsoft-US7664735-SearchDiversityRanking.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Re-ranks a result set using document-to-document affinity so the final ordering trades raw relevance against diversity/information richness — near-duplicate results are pushed apart instead of stacking the top of the list. Claims cover the affinity-based re-ranking apparatus and method.
- TRANSFER: A concrete, implementable recipe for diversifying any ranked output GSE ships — content feeds, recommended reads, package lineups — where ten near-identical items in the top slots destroy the funnel. Affinity-matrix re-ranking is computable from embeddings the stack already produces.

title: 4. Google Inc. — US 8,572,075 B1 (2013) — 21 pp
text:
**"Framework for Evaluating Web Search Scoring Functions"** (inventors incl. Paul Haahr, Matt Cutts). File: `Google-US8572075-EvaluatingSearchScoringFunctions.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: An offline evaluation harness for ranking functions: candidate ("alpha"/"beta") scoring functions are run over queries, their top results compared, and a *diversity score* between the two orderings is calculated so a new scoring function is judged by how its output actually differs and performs before it ships. Claims cover the comparison/diversity measurement pipeline.
- TRANSFER: This is an A/B discipline for ranking changes, written by the team that ran Google search quality: never ship a scoring change you cannot first diff against the incumbent offline. Maps one-to-one onto GSE's verdict-gate practice for engine changes — candidate vs incumbent, diff measured, ship decision second.

## PATENTS — Recommendation / affiliate / funnel / pricing

section: 5. Amazon.com, Inc. — US 6,266,649 B1 (2001) — 22 pp
title: 5. Amazon.com, Inc. — US 6,266,649 B1 (2001) — 22 pp
text:
**"Collaborative Recommendations Using Item-to-Item Similarity Mappings"** (inventors incl. Greg Linden, Brent Smith). File: `Amazon-US6266649-ItemToItemCF.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Precomputes item-to-item similarity mappings offline from user purchase/rating co-occurrence, then generates recommendations in real time by matching a user's known items against the mapping — the item-to-item collaborative filtering architecture Amazon still describes as its recommender core. Claims cover the similarity-mapping generation and the recommendation method built on it.
- TRANSFER: The cheapest recommender architecture that actually works at scale: precompute similarity once, serve lookups forever. For GSE content and package surfaces ("readers of this slate also took…"), item-to-item CF over content/packages needs no user model and no cold-start machinery — directly buildable from existing interaction data.

section: 6. Amazon.com, Inc. — US 6,029,141 (2000) — 28 pp
title: 6. Amazon.com, Inc. — US 6,029,141 (2000) — 28 pp
text:
**"Internet-Based Customer Referral System"** (the Associates-program patent). File: `Amazon-US6029141-CustomerReferralSystem.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: A store site issues associates personalized links carrying an associate identifier; when a referred customer purchases, the system credits the sale to the associate from the identifier carried through the session/URL, and reports earnings back to the associate. Claims cover the referral-link issuance, identifier-based purchase crediting, and associate reporting method.
- TRANSFER: The canonical affiliate-tracking design, in claims form: identifier in the link, credit at purchase, transparent reporting. This is the exact mechanism GSE's live affiliate accounts (Amazon Associates tag `galaxysportse-20`, OddsJam, Impact) implement from the other side — reading the merchant-side claims shows precisely which events are creditable and where attribution can silently break (identifier dropped mid-session = lost commission).

section: 7. Intellions, Inc. — US 7,330,839 B2 (2008) — 13 pp
title: 7. Intellions, Inc. — US 7,330,839 B2 (2008) — 13 pp
text:
**"Method and System for Dynamic Pricing"** (inventors Kannan Srinivasan, Michael Shamos — CMU). File: `Intellions-US7330839-DynamicPricing.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Determines an optimal web price by running controlled short-term price experiments: the merchant configures a sample size of visitors and experiment timing, the system exposes sampled visitors to test prices, measures conversion response, and computes the revenue-optimal price from measured price sensitivity. Claims cover the experiment configuration, sampling, and optimal-price determination pipeline.
- TRANSFER: Pricing by experiment, not by opinion — the governed way to test GSE's package prices ($29–$49 today) instead of guessing: small sampled price cells, measured conversion, pick the optimum. Note the claims' discipline: sample size and duration are set *before* the experiment runs, which is the part most informal price tests skip.

## PATENTS — Sports / betting (round 2, all new)

section: 8. Stats LLC (Stats Perform) — US 12,367,244 B2 (2025) — 37 pp
title: 8. Stats LLC (Stats Perform) — US 12,367,244 B2 (2025) — 37 pp
text:
**"System and Methods for Implementing a Feature Set of High-Dimensional Spatial Data in Sports Predictions"** (inventors incl. Patrick Lucey). File: `StatsLLC-US12367244-SpatialDataSportsPredictions.pdf`. Front page verified by image render from the shelved PDF.
- CLAIMS: Generates an action probability in two stages: an ML model produces an initial projected scoring probability from a minimal input (positions of a first player and a target area), then a richer feature set — second-player positions, distances and angles between players and target, tracking-derived quantities — *modifies* that probability into an updated scoring probability. Claims cover the two-stage feature-set refinement method (10 claims).
- TRANSFER: This is the incumbent tracking-data prediction architecture (Lucey's group) written as claims: a baseline probability refined by spatial context features. It is the benchmark shape for any GSE tracking-derived feature work — and a freedom-to-operate read: the two-stage "initial probability → spatial feature refinement" pattern is claimed, so GSE's implementations should document their own differing construction.

section: 9. Intel Corporation — US 11,049,031 B2 (2021) — 21 pp
title: 9. Intel Corporation — US 11,049,031 B2 (2021) — 21 pp
text:
**"Methods and Apparatus to Predict Sports Injuries."** File: `Intel-US11049031-PredictSportsInjuries.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Predicts a target player's injury probability for a target date by combining three components: (1) injury probabilities of *similar* players (similarity from performance/fitness data over 7/14/30-day windows in an associative memory base), (2) the target player's own injury history, and (3) a fused probability from the two, emitted as a report. Claims cover the similar-athlete retrieval plus probability-fusion method.
- TRANSFER: A complete, buildable injury-risk recipe that does not need wearables: similar-player priors fused with personal history, over rolling windows. It complements (does not duplicate) round 1's Catapult load patent — Catapult claims load measurement; Intel claims the prediction layer on top of ordinary performance data GSE already has.

section: 10. Action Network, Inc. → Better Collective USA, Inc. — US 11,681,937 B2 (2023) — 10 pp
title: 10. Action Network, Inc. → Better Collective USA, Inc. — US 11,681,937 B2 (2023) — 10 pp
text:
**"System, Method, and Platform for Generating a Real-Time Bet Win Probability."** File: `BetterCollective-US11681937-RealTimeBetWinProbability.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Stores a user's wager, trains a model on historical data to predict the probability that a bet type wins over the course of a game, then compares the stored wager against live in-game data to generate and update a real-time win probability for that specific bet. Claims cover the wager-storage → live-data comparison → per-bet probability update loop.
- TRANSFER: The product pattern behind live bet-tracking content: per-user, per-bet live win probability as an engagement surface. For GSE it is a content/funnel blueprint (live probability on a published pick is a retention feature) and a competitive-intel read on what Better Collective considers worth claiming.

section: 11. Verizon Media Inc. → Yahoo Assets LLC — US 10,967,281 B2 (2021) — 26 pp
title: 11. Verizon Media Inc. → Yahoo Assets LLC — US 10,967,281 B2 (2021) — 26 pp
text:
**"Automatic Fantasy Sports Data Analysis Method and Apparatus"** (inventors incl. Maxim Sviridenko, Justin Thaler). File: `Yahoo-US10967281-FantasySportsDataAnalysis.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Determines fantasy salaries for a contest from multiple factors and performs automatic analysis to *equalize player attractiveness* across contestants — adjusting the salary/analysis outputs so contestants do not all draft near-identical lineups. Claims cover the salary determination and attractiveness-equalization analysis method.
- TRANSFER: The operator-side view of DFS: salaries exist to spread ownership, not just to price talent. For GSE's DFS packages, the exploitable gap is exactly the difference between salary-implied value and ownership-equalized value — this patent states the operator's objective function, which tells you where the field's lineups will cluster.

## PATENTS — AI / agents

section: 12. SAP AG (now SAP SE) — US 7,437,703 B2 (2008) — 30 pp
title: 12. SAP AG (now SAP SE) — US 7,437,703 B2 (2008) — 30 pp
text:
**"Enterprise Multi-Agent Software System."** File: `SAP-US7437703-EnterpriseMultiAgentSystem.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: A multi-agent environment built from callable core service modules (each performing a core function against a data source) plus intelligent service modules that invoke engines; a core function stores work in a *scheduling time sheet*, so agents coordinate through shared services and a scheduler rather than ad-hoc calls. Claims cover the service-module architecture, the multi-engine invocation, and the scheduling capability.
- TRANSFER: A reference architecture for the agent fleet's coordination layer: shared services + explicit scheduling as the coordination substrate. Dated (2003 priority) but the claimed decomposition — dumb reliable core services, smart thin agents, scheduler in the middle — is the same shape as the fleet MCP bus, and the patent is expired/near expiry, so it is safe prior art to design against.

section: 13. IBM (now Maplebear Inc.) — US 7,483,986 B2 (2009) — 14 pp
title: 13. IBM (now Maplebear Inc.) — US 7,483,986 B2 (2009) — 14 pp
text:
**"Dynamically Tuning Networks of Relationships in Self-Organizing Multi-Agent Systems."** File: `IBM-US7483986-SelfOrganizingMultiAgentTopology.pdf`.
- CLAIMS: Self-organizing agents autonomously form connectivity relationships representable as a degree-distribution topology; a topology tuner measures the topology against system criteria and recommends/adjusts relationship changes so the agent network's connectivity stays near a target distribution. Claims cover the topology establishment and tuning method.
- TRANSFER: The formal version of a live fleet question: which agents should talk to which, and how densely? Degree-distribution tuning gives a measurable target for fleet routing topology instead of vibes — relevant to any future change in how the fleet's agents hand work to each other.

section: 1. MS MARCO (passage ranking / QA) — Microsoft, via Hugging Face
title: 1. MS MARCO (passage ranking / QA) — Microsoft, via Hugging Face
text:
- HOST: Hugging Face `microsoft/ms_marco` (official Microsoft org); origin: Microsoft Research, paper arXiv:1611.09268.
- LICENSE: MS MARCO research terms via Microsoft (dataset card carries no HF license tag; use governed by Microsoft's MS MARCO terms — research use).
- SCALE / FORMAT: Parquet on HF. Two configs: v1.1 (100K real Bing questions w/ human answers) and v2.1 (1M-question corpus).
- VERIFIED FACT (HF API, this run): v2.1 splits — train 808,731 / validation 101,093 / test 101,092 examples; v1.1 — train 82,326 / validation 10,047 / test 9,650; features are `query`, `answers`, and `passages` with `is_selected` relevance labels and source URLs; 21,427 downloads recorded.
- TRANSFER: The standard training/eval corpus for retrieval and ranking models — the labeled query→passage relevance data for teaching any GSE search/retrieval surface (site search, corpus search over the research library) what a good ranking looks like, with the `is_selected` label as ground truth.

section: 2. Amazon Reviews 2023 — McAuley Lab, UC San Diego
title: 2. Amazon Reviews 2023 — McAuley Lab, UC San Diego
text:
- HOST: Hugging Face `McAuley-Lab/Amazon-Reviews-2023` + official project page amazon-reviews-2023.github.io (UCSD datarepo links were dead at the checked path — see GAPS).
- LICENSE: No formal license assigned — the lab states it is not in a position to assign one or dictate terms; distributed for research use. (Third-party blogs claiming "CC BY-NC 4.0" are not the lab's own statement.)
- SCALE / FORMAT: JSONL per category (34 category files, ~275 GB total), plus item metadata and user-item link graphs. Reviews May 1996 – Sep 2023.
- VERIFIED FACT (official project page stats table, this run): **571.54M reviews, 54.51M users, 48.19M items, 33 categories**, with second-level timestamps — 245.2% larger than the 2018 release.
- TRANSFER: The training ground for review/recommendation models at real scale: rating + text + metadata + bought-together graphs in one corpus. For GSE's affiliate/content work it is the dataset for learning what review language converts — and for item-to-item CF experiments (patent #5 above) with real co-purchase links.

section: 3. RetailRocket Recommender System Dataset — Kaggle
title: 3. RetailRocket Recommender System Dataset — Kaggle
text:
- HOST: Kaggle, `retailrocket/ecommerce-dataset` (file download requires a Kaggle account; metadata below verified from Kaggle's own structured dataset record, this run).
- LICENSE: **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** (stated in Kaggle's structured metadata).
- SCALE / FORMAT: Three CSVs — `events.csv`, `item_properties.csv` (split in two parts), `category_tree.csv`; 4.5 months of real e-commerce behavior; all IDs hashed.
- VERIFIED FACT (Kaggle metadata): **2,756,101 events = 2,664,312 views + 69,332 add-to-carts + 22,457 transactions, from 1,407,580 unique visitors**; ~90% of events have matching item properties.
- TRANSFER: A complete view→cart→transaction funnel with timestamps — the practice dataset for funnel-conversion modeling (session features → purchase probability) that maps directly onto GSE's own package funnel questions, with a real category tree for hierarchical features.

section: 4. MovieLens 25M — GroupLens, University of Minnesota
title: 4. MovieLens 25M — GroupLens, University of Minnesota
text:
- HOST: GroupLens official (grouplens.org / files.grouplens.org), direct download, no auth.
- LICENSE: GroupLens research terms — provided for research/education use; redistribution requires GroupLens permission; not a commercial-use license.
- SCALE / FORMAT: Six CSVs — `ratings.csv`, `tags.csv`, `movies.csv`, `links.csv`, `genome-scores.csv`, `genome-tags.csv`.
- VERIFIED FACT (official ml-25m README, this run): **25,000,095 ratings and 1,093,360 tag applications across 62,423 movies by 162,541 users** (Jan 1995 – Nov 2019; generated Nov 21, 2019), plus a 1,128-tag relevance genome.
- TRANSFER: The cleanest labeled preference data in existence for validating a recommender before touching real users: if a CF or ranking change cannot beat baselines on MovieLens 25M, it does not ship. The tag genome is also a worked example of interpretable content features — the same pattern GSE needs for explainable pick/content features.

section: 5. Common Crawl Web Graphs (host- and domain-level) — Common Crawl
title: 5. Common Crawl Web Graphs (host- and domain-level) — Common Crawl
text:
- HOST: data.commoncrawl.org/projects/hyperlinkgraph/ (release index at index.commoncrawl.org/web-graphs-index.html).
- LICENSE: Free under Common Crawl's Terms of Use.
- SCALE / FORMAT: Per release: host graph + domain graph as gzipped vertex/edge text files (`<id, reversed host>` vertices, `<from_id, to_id>` edges), plus ranking/statistics files.
- VERIFIED FACT (latest release page cc-main-2026-aug-sep-oct, this run): **host-level graph = 242.8M nodes and 2.4B edges** (178.6M dangling nodes, 73.55%; largest SCC 38.6M nodes); domain-vertices file 7.1 GiB, domain-edges 3.8 GiB.
- TRANSFER: The open web's actual link graph — PageRank (patent #1) computable at web scale without crawling anything. For GSE's "be seen by search engines" lane this is the measurement instrument: where galaxysportsedge.com and its niche sit in the real graph, which hosts link into the category, and which link targets would move the domain's graph position — facts, not SEO opinion.

section: 6. StatsBomb Open Data — StatsBomb (Hudl)
title: 6. StatsBomb Open Data — StatsBomb (Hudl)
text:
- HOST: GitHub `statsbomb/open-data` (repository now under the `hudl` org after acquisition; resolves by redirect).
- LICENSE: NOASSERTION in GitHub metadata — StatsBomb's own terms in the repo: free to use with attribution and their stated conditions; not an OSI license.
- SCALE / FORMAT: JSON — `competitions.json`, per-match events (360 freeze-frame data for a subset), lineups, and match files; ~7.6 GB repository.
- VERIFIED FACT (this run, from the data itself): `competitions.json` contains **80 competition-seasons across 24 unique competitions** (men's and women's, incl. full World Cups and top-5 European leagues).
- TRANSFER: Event-level soccer data with a stable schema — the training/eval set for any GSE soccer modeling and, more importantly, a reference event schema: how a professional data provider structures events, freezes, and lineups is the template for GSE's own event-data contracts in other sports.

section: AM-01 — FreeToken: edge-native MoE serving engine — @simplifyinai (recreator)
title: AM-01 — FreeToken: edge-native MoE serving engine — @simplifyinai (recreator)
text:
Post: https://www.instagram.com/p/DfWsgp9GU5t/ (carousel, 2026-11-05 01:20 CT) · Feed position 40
1. **WHAT IT IS** — An open-source serving engine that runs frontier-scale Mixture-of-Experts models on a personal machine by treating GPU + CPU + system RAM + interconnect as one elastic inference platform: bandwidth-adaptive CPU–GPU co-execution, a global LRU expert cache, streamed prefill, and a fast weight format. Because an MoE activates only a few experts per token (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 6 of 256 routed experts per layer ≈ 13B of 284B active), most weights can live outside VRAM and be filled or computed in place on cache miss. Ships as a Windows/Linux desktop app and a Python package, with OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints (`ft serve`, port 1919) and `ft launch claude` wiring for Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode.
2. **WHERE TO FIND IT** — Repo: https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken · Paper: arXiv:2608.16157, "FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution" (UC Berkeley / UT Austin; authors include Song Han, Matei Zaharia, Ion Stoica) · Download: flashml.ai · PyPI: `freetoken` v0.1.2 (`uv pip install "freetoken[accel]"`). The Instagram poster @simplifyinai is a recreator; the paper + repo are the origin.
3. **HOW TO USE IT** — Desktop app (Windows/Linux) or CLI. CLI requirements per repo coverage: Linux x86_64, NVIDIA GPU, driver r580+, Python 3.10+, CUDA 13 toolkit. Supported: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GLM-5.2 (+20 MoE models per paper) in MXFP4/NVFP4/FP8/BF16. Hardware named: NVIDIA RTX 30/40/50-series; AMD support is work-in-progress.
4. **WHICH SYSTEM IT PLUGS INTO** — Model-routing stack + agent fleet infrastructure. section: AM-02 — Edge0: SSD-streamed MoE inference, 35B in 2.9 GB — @reporadarai (recreator)
title: AM-02 — Edge0: SSD-streamed MoE inference, 35B in 2.9 GB — @reporadarai (recreator)
text:
Post: https://www.instagram.com/p/DfIh8osD0LP/ (2026-10-30) · Feed position 49
1. **WHAT IT IS** — An open-source inference framework that runs a 35B-parameter MoE model with ~2.9 GiB peak *active* memory by memory-mapping expert weights from SSD and streaming only the experts a token needs. Three mechanisms per its docs: SSD expert offload (`SafetensorsMmap` + a cross-layer LRU `SharedExpertCache`), a trained per-layer **prerouter** that predicts the next token's experts one step ahead (the source of the claimed up-to-59% decode boost), and an unmerged LoRA that recovers most int4 quantization loss. Ships two checkpoints: `Edge0-35B-A3B-preview` (from Qwen3.5-MoE) and `Edge0-8B-A1B-preview` (from Ling-3.0-tiny). Measured in project material: 2.9 GiB / 20.4 tok/s for 35B vs 18.2 GiB for a fully resident int4 engine.
2. **WHERE TO FIND IT** — Repo (linked in the post itself): https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Edge0 · Paper: "The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction." Poster @reporadarai is a recreator/aggregator.
3. **HOW TO USE IT** — **macOS on Apple Silicon only in this release** (M1–M4), via its MLX backend (`mlx==0.30.6`, `mlx-lm==0.31.0` pinned). CUDA backend is roadmap, not shipped. Disk: ~23 GB for the 35B checkpoint (stays on disk, memory-mapped), ~4.2 GB for 8B. Known issue: newer MLX builds garble output on A18/A18 Pro — the pin is the fix (repo issue #8).

Preview quality is explicitly not yet aimed at agentic-task quality, so it fits reading, triage, and summarization seats, not the reasoning seat.

title: AM-03 — API Anything: turn any website into an API for agents — @charles.zhengg (originator)
text:
Post: https://www.instagram.com/p/DeON0MOB5oi/ (2026-10-07) · Feed position 34
1. **WHAT IT IS** — A tool that learns a website's *internal* network requests and re-exposes them as operations an agent calls over HTTP, skipping browser automation entirely. Learning method: load the same page twice with two different values in a headless browser; the part of the request that changes becomes the parameter. Calls then run in tiers, starting with a direct Node `fetch` (no browser). Learned operations go into a shared catalog (a Cloudflare Worker stores specs and success/fail votes — it never proxies traffic; calls leave from your machine, logins stay local). Ships ~30 read operations across 14 sites (Goodreads, Google Flights, Hacker News, LinkedIn, X, Instagram, others). The poster is the project's author (Charles Zheng), demonstrating his own tool — provenance is first-party here.
2. **WHERE TO FIND IT** — Repo (shown in the video): https://github.com/goodnight000/api-anything · npm package `api-anything`, v0.2.0 (2026-10-28) · Independent test: jacar.es API Anything review (tested 2026-10-28, arm64 Linux). MIT license.
3. **HOW TO USE IT** — Install via npm; requires Node 22.13+. Connects as an MCP server to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Claude Desktop. Teach it a site with the `add` flow (e.g. `api-anything add hn-demo links`); an operation goes live in the shared catalog after installs on 2 other networks call it successfully, and is replaced after 3+ networks see it fail.

section: AM-04 — ECC (Everything Claude Code): agent harness OS — @ericdoestech (recreator)
title: AM-04 — ECC (Everything Claude Code): agent harness OS — @ericdoestech (recreator)
text:
Post: https://www.instagram.com/p/DdwJADlBFnX/ (2026-09-26) · Feed position 57
1. **WHAT IT IS** — A large, MIT-licensed configuration system for Claude Code: a catalog of specialized subagents, skills, slash commands, hooks, rules, and a memory vault that installs in one command and imposes a `plan → test → implement → review → verify → remember → improve` loop. The reel's snapshot (64 agents / 261 skills / 84 commands, ~262k stars) is already stale — later independent counts of the same repo read 68 agents / 286–311 skills / 94–97 commands, which tells you the repo moves weekly. Author: Affaan Mustafa (Anthropic hackathon winner, per multiple profiles). A paid hosted tier (ECC Pro, per-seat) funds it; the repo itself is free.
2. **WHERE TO FIND IT** — Repo: https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC · Plugin: `ecc@ecc` · npm: `ecc-universal`. Install from the official repo only — the README itself warns unofficial mirrors may carry malware. Independent deep audit: aidive.dev's token audit of v2.2.1.
3. **HOW TO USE IT** — `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` then `/plugin install ecc@ecc`, or `npx ecc-universal setup`. Adapters exist for Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini and others with reduced capability.

WHAT IT IS — A research system, verified at secondary/primary sources: SwaT trains a small mapper that translates one frozen LLM's KV-cache into another model family's KV-cache format, so a receiving model can continue from the sender's internal state without the sender's context ever being converted to text (prefill-free handoff). The poster is a recreator/summarizer; the paper and repo are the original source.

text: Post: https://x.com/miyashita_03/status/2118328415258608063 (feed #9). title: Racelighting through branded entertainment: the historical case of the National Football League
text:
Purpose The purpose of the paper is to draw on the American National Football League (NFL’s) century-plus history, as documented in media meta-texts, to examine how race is deployed in its branded entertainment (BE) marketing strategy. In this viewpoint article, the authors extend “racelighting” (RL) as a conceptual framework to illuminate approaches in which BE marketing strategies – often conveyed as neutral or progressive – leverage racial stereotypes to exploit the cultural, social and political capital of black and other persons of color to align with the commercial interests of dominant groups in ways that ultimately undermine progressive movements. Design/methodology/approach While football game outcomes tell the narrative of NFL-BE as surface text, meta-texts comprise the plethora of marketing content produced about the games and the league. This paper examines the topic using a thematic analysis perspective and archival evidence, classifying media meta-texts along three binary, coded themes for distribution channels, forms of hegemonic control and marketing strategy. This study compiled 20 articles from the Crisis magazine (1910–1960), 25 from Ebony magazine (1945–2026), 21 from Jet magazine (1950–2015) and six transcripts of audio/visual NFL-branded content (2014–2026), organized chronologically under historical thematic categories. These 72 meta-texts include the following US time periods: the post-Reconstruction Jim Crow era (1910–1949), the Civil Rights era (1950–1979), the rise of neoliberal colorblindness era (1980–2008) and the post-racial era (2009–2026). Findings Through historical analysis aided by semiotics, the authors illuminate how RL has adapted over the NFL’s century-long history to maintain narrative control and secure its dominant cultural and hegemonic position. Grounding their analysis through the lens of Afro-pessimism that advocates the centering of black voices and perspectives, they reveal the NFL’s reality-distorting RL-BE strategy

title: Supervised LSTM Sequence-to-Sequence Models for NFL Player Trajectory Prediction: A Deep Learning Approach to the Big Data Bowl 2026
text: Abstract The NFL Big Data Bowl 2026 challenges participants to predict player trajectories during pass plays using Next Gen Stats data. We present a purely supervised LSTM sequence-to-sequence approach optimized via Hyperband on Z-score normalized features. Our model design is contextualized by analyzing 18,009 pass plays and validated through 981 automated hypothesis-driven experiments. These experiments revealed critical biomechanical constraints, including restricted directional freedom at high speeds (p < 0.001) and significant orientation–movement mismatches for defensive players (103.8°, p < 0.001). Facilitated by a memory-efficient Polars preprocessing pipeline, our systematic optimization of data normalization and hyperparameters reduced prediction error by 81.4%, improving our initial RMSE from 50.335 to a best score of 9.338 RMSE. Our findings demonstrate that rigorous data normalization—specifically Z-scoring—combined with systematic hyperparameter search outweighs model complexity. Alternative semi-supervised paradigms were explored as ablation studies and found to underperform the supervised baseline once normalization was applied.
